understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call anger that takes over, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.week_thesis: The anger the news feeds becomes, over seven days, something you can meet without being carried by it.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the anger and the replaying as a felt state, named without blame.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the anger rises from a wanting that cannot be satisfied, and that the mind is never given one quiet minute to settle.
week_beats.steady: You hold that what is real in you cannot be shaken by what is shown on the screen.
week_beats.act: You try one hour without the phone, and when the anger rises, you let it pass without speaking or acting.
week_beats.story: A warrior who faced an army that would not listen shows you how to fight only what is in front of you.

understanding.core_struggle: Spends five hours on the phone replaying the news, and is angry at the other side every day.
understanding.mirror: You open the news and the anger rises, then you keep going back to it.
understanding.insight: The anger arrives before you choose it. By the time you notice, it has already spoken for you.

queries.hook: The anger that rises every time you open the news, and the replaying that keeps you stuck in it.
queries.diagnose: When desire is blocked, anger rises and clouds judgement; the mind that is clouded says and does what it later regrets.
queries.steady: Praise and blame come and go, and what is real in you cannot be shaken by what is said or shown.
queries.act: Practise one hour of the day with the phone away, and when the anger rises, let it pass without speaking or acting.
queries.story: A warrior who faced an army that would not listen, and chose to fight only what was in front of him.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse.sanskrit: चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम् । तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम् ॥
verse.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.
verse.why: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

matched.label: I feel anxious most of the time

prasang.title: Mastering the mind
prasang.summary: Arjuna says the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn. Krishna agrees, and says practice and letting go can train it.
prasang.lesson: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

verse.meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield, saying the mind is restless, turbulent and strong. He says holding it feels like trying to grasp the wind. Krishna does not argue. He agrees that the mind is hard to hold, but he says it can be trained through practice and letting go.
verse.for_you: The anger you feel at the news and the hours you spend scrolling are not a failure. They are the wind Krishna speaks of, and your mind is simply caught in its current.
verse.try_today: Notice the anger arriving before you choose it.
verse.scene_line: You are on the battlefield, and the mind is the wind.
asks: How do I stop the mind from becoming the wind?
How do I let go of a feeling that feels so real?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse.sanskrit: ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते । सङ्गात् संजायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ॥
verse.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.
verse.why: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

prasang.title: The person of steady wisdom
prasang.summary: Arjuna asks how a steady person speaks, sits and walks. Krishna describes someone content within, unshaken by sorrow, master of the senses, and traces how dwelling on things leads to anger and ruin.
prasang.lesson: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

verse.meaning: Krishna is answering Arjuna, who wants to know what a steady mind looks like. He says it begins with where you let your eyes and thoughts rest. If you keep dwelling on what you see and want, attachment grows. When that wanting is blocked, it hardens into anger. The mind is never allowed a quiet minute because it is always chasing what it has attached to.
verse.for_you: The news cycle keeps offering you things to want and then blocks them, so the anger has nowhere to go. Your mind is not broken. It is just never left alone with itself. Notice what you are dwelling on before it becomes wanting.
verse.try_today: When the anger rises, name the last thing you saw on the phone that fed it.
verse.scene_line: You are dwelling on the news and it has turned into wanting and then anger.
asks: How do I stop my mind from dwelling on the news?
Can I change what I let my mind rest on?

verse.speaker: Teacher
verse.setting: Rules of conduct for a renunciant.
verse.sanskrit: नात्यर्थं सुखदुःखाभ्यां शरीरमुपतायेत् । स्तूयमानो न तुषेत निन्दितो न शपेत्परान् ॥
verse.line: Don't wear out your body chasing pleasure or fleeing pain. Praised, don't gloat; blamed, don't curse others.
verse.translation: Let him not torment the body too much for the sake of pleasure or pain. Praised, let him not gloat; blamed, let him not curse others.
verse.meaning: A teacher tells a renunciant how to live in the world without being torn apart by it. The renunciant is learning to let go of extremes. The teacher says do not wear out the body by chasing pleasure or running from pain. If people praise you, do not let it swell you up. If they blame you, do not let it turn into a curse against them. The point is to keep the body steady and the heart even, no matter which way the wind blows.
verse.for_you: Your body is not a weapon for the news cycle. You scroll for five hours and the anger sits in your chest like a second job. You do not have to prove anything to the screen. You can let the headlines move through you without letting them wear you out.
verse.try_today: Notice the body's first sign of anger before the mind names it.
verse.scene_line: You are the renunciant, praised by the screen, blamed by the screen.
asks: How do I stop the body from wearing out?
How do I praise without gloating?

verse.speaker: Vidura
verse.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
verse.sanskrit: न हृष्यत्यात्मसंमाने नावमानेन तप्यते / गाङ्गो ह्रद इवाक्षोभ्यो यः स पण्डित उच्यते
verse.line: Don't swell with praise or burn at a slight; stay deep and still like a river pool.
verse.translation: One who is not elated when honoured, nor pained when slighted, and who stays unruffled like a deep pool of the Ganga, is called wise.
verse.why: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

prasang.title: Vidura Niti: the wise and the fool
prasang.summary: Sleepless before the peace talks, King Dhritarashtra calls his half-brother Vidura for counsel. Vidura describes the marks of the wise and the fool, the faults that block progress, and the six joys of life.
prasang.lesson: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

verse.for_you: The news you scroll is praise and blame, and it is making you burn. But the anger you feel is not the whole of you. There is a steady part that watches the screen without being swallowed by it. You can return to that quiet depth.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment when the anger rises and let it pass without feeding it.
verse.scene_line: You stand in your own room, holding the phone like a mirror of outrage.
asks: What is the steady part of me that the screen cannot touch?
How do I tell the news from the feeling it creates?
Can I sit with the anger without letting it decide my hour?

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Yudhishthira
verse.setting: In exile, Draupadi urges Yudhishthira to answer injustice with force; he argues for forgiveness.
verse.sanskrit: आत्मानं च परांश्चैव त्रायते महतो भयात् / क्रुध्यन्तमप्रतिक्रुध्यन्दूयोरेष चिकित्सकः
verse.line: Don't answer anger with anger. The one who stays calm protects both people, and heals both.
verse.translation: One who does not get angry back at an angry person saves both himself and the other from great danger. He becomes the healer of both.
verse.why: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.
verse.misuse: Staying calm is not the same as staying in a situation where you are unsafe.

prasang.title: Forgiveness or force: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
prasang.summary: In the forest, Draupadi asks why Yudhishthira does not answer injustice with anger, citing Prahlada's advice that neither force nor forgiveness is always right. Yudhishthira replies that anger destroys and forgiveness holds the world together.
prasang.story_hook: Thirteen years into exile, Draupadi looked at her husband and asked why he was not angry.
prasang.lesson: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.

verse.for_you: Pause before you speak, hold back the harsh word, and answer anger with calm; forgive so the fire does not keep burning in you.

verse.speaker: Ribhu
verse.setting: Ribhu on inner stillness in an active life.
verse.sanskrit: बहिःकृत्रिमसंरंभो हृदि संरम्भवर्जितः । कर्ता बहिरकर्तान्तर्लोके विहर शुद्धधीः ॥
verse.line: Be busy on the outside and unhurried inside. Act fully, but don't let it agitate you.
verse.translation: Outwardly busy, inwardly free of agitation; a doer on the outside, a non-doer within: move through the world with a clear mind.
verse.why: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

matched.label: I feel anxious most of the time

prasang.title: How a free person lives
prasang.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.
prasang.lesson: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

verse.for_you: Anger is a passing fire in the mind; you can watch it rise and fall without letting it speak for you.

story.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
story.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
story.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

anchor.speaker: Janaka
anchor.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
anchor.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
anchor.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
anchor.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
anchor.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
anchor.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.
